bib.title: ContinualSkillBench: Can LLM Agents Truly Evolve Their Capabilities?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: ContinualSkillBench: Can LLM Agents Truly Evolve Their Capabilities? Guan, Wang, Yang, Cao, Liu, Hu, Li, Zhang (Peking Univ. / BIGAI). arXiv 2608.03874v3, 15 Oct 2026, preprint (ACL-style format, no venue stated).

COVERAGE: Read the main text, limitations and references in full (about 0-48,000 of 90,384 chars). In the appendices I read B-C by targeted scan (human validation, skill-recurrence tables), D prompt intro, and F-H in full. I did not read Table 10 (the RAG ablation numbers), only its prose, and I did not read Appendix E line by line. I did not run the figure-caption script. I read the two note sections only as far as their headings, tables and first lines of each paragraph. No extraction faults and no embedded instructions.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Explicit skill maintenance gives no aggregate gain over just keeping context and feedback.
 number: normalized reward 0.469 (Independent), 0.585 (pure ICL), 0.582 (Sequential with skills)
 setup: GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude 4.7 Opus, Law/Finance/Healthcare, 100 ordered tasks per domain, 6 model-domain combinations. ICL gets the same sequence and evaluator feedback but cannot create or modify skills.
 quote: "the normalized rewards of Independent, ICL, and skill-maintaining Sequential execution are 0.469, 0.585, and 0.582, respectively."
 where: Sec 4.3, p8

2. Retaining experience across tasks generally helps, but unevenly.
 number: +0.071 raw and +0.078 normalized, macro-averaged over 15 model-domain pairs (16.2% and 16.9% relative)
 setup: GPT-4o, GPT-5.3-Codex, Opus 4.7 on Law, Finance, Healthcare, Office, Math. Sequential vs Independent, where Independent resets history and skills before each task. This combines retained context, feedback and skills.
 quote: "Sequential execution increases raw reward in 13 of the 15 model–domain combinations and normalized reward in 14 of 15. Macro-averaged across all combinations, the absolute improvements are +0.071 in raw reward and +0.078 in normalized reward."
 where: Sec 4.2, p7. (The intro says "improves in 14 of 15", which is the normalized count.) Healthcare has the largest average normalized gain (+0.149); the only normalized drop is Opus 4.7 on Math (-0.008).

3. Skills help on rigid-format and procedural tasks. Context-only does better on open-ended rubric tasks.
 number: Sequential beats or ties ICL on Exact Match in 6 of 6 comparisons (5 better, 1 tie), matches or beats it on Programmatic in 5 of 6, and ICL has higher Rubric scores in 5 of 6.
 setup: same as claim 1. The RAG-over-trajectories baseline in App. F shows the same pattern, but I did not read its table.
 quote: "Sequential improves Exact Match performance in five of the six comparisons and ties ICL in the remaining one; it also matches or outperforms ICL on Programmatic tasks in five of six comparisons. Conversely, ICL obtains higher Rubric scores in five of six comparisons."
 where: Sec 4.3, p8. The authors' reading: skills "may over-specialize to earlier solution patterns on open-ended tasks."

4. The weaker model builds more skills, reuses them less, and writes lower-quality ones.
 number: 384 skills at average quality 5.68 (GPT-4o) vs 205 skills at 7.94 (GPT-5.3-Codex)
 setup: all 5 domains, skills scored by GPT-4.1-mini on a rubric. Score = format × content, and an invalid YAML header scores 0. Skill counts exclude meta-skills. Fig 3 call frequency gives GPT-5.3-Codex 225 calls in one domain against 79 for GPT-4o in the first domain listed. The extraction does not label which bar is which domain, so I am not citing it.
 quote: "GPT-4o produces a much larger number of skills across domains (384 in total), but their average quality score is substantially lower (5.68). In contrast, GPT-5.3-Codex maintains a smaller skill pool (205 skills) with consistently higher quality (7.94 on average)."
 where: App. G, p20-21, supporting Sec 4.4 on skill fragmentation.

5. Skill-pool growth is not learning. A compact, reused library beats a large one.
 number: none beyond claim 4
 quote: "GPT-4o exhibits the opposite behavior: it accumulates a larger skill pool but invokes the resulting skills less frequently."
 where: Sec 4.4, p8

6. The ordered streams really do offer reuse opportunities, which supports reading the null result in claim 1 as real.
 number: 69.5% of eligible tasks reuse at least one earlier core skill, and 35.5% of core-skill needs are covered by prior history. Curated order gives 25.7% local coverage vs 20.4% for random order (+5.3 points) in a 5-task window.
 quote: "69.5% of eligible tasks reuse at least one previously encountered core skill, while 35.5% of their core-skill requirements are covered by the preceding history, macro-averaged across domains."
 where: Sec 3.3, p5. The 89% agreement between human annotators and the LLM judge on 400 sampled dependency calls is in Sec 3.2.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: the tasks come from a fixed set of sources and miss long-tail and distribution-shift cases. Only a few models and harnesses were run (Codex CLI and Claude Code). There was no Gemini, Cursor or other environment, and API cost was the reason.
- The ICL-vs-skills ablation covers only 2 models and 3 domains (not Office or Math).
- The skill-reuse and fragmentation analysis (Fig 3) covers only GPT-4o and GPT-5.3-Codex, not Opus 4.7.
- Reward is mixed: LLM-judged rubrics, LLM-assisted task ordering, and LLM-scored skill quality.
- Per-domain subsets are small. Some Exact Match cells rest on about 10 to 14 tasks, which is my inference from the values (for example 0.364, 0.455) and not stated by the authors.
- Raw and normalized reward can disagree, because normalized reward is computed over valid outputs only.
- No variance, seeds or significance tests are reported for the model comparisons.
- Skills are SKILL.md files under a prompted create/modify protocol, not a learned memory manager. Relevance to MemGPT-style block memory is by analogy.

BUILDS ON
- Skills and tool learning: Schick et al. 2023 (Toolformer); Shen et al. 2023 (HuggingGPT); Xu and Yan 2026 (agent skills survey).
- Expert-written skills help: Li et al. 2026 (SkillsBench).
- Skill-learning benchmarks: Zhong et al. 2026 (SkillLearnBench); Asawa et al. 2026 (Continual Learning Bench); Dou et al. 2026 (CL-bench); Chen et al. 2026 (SkillCraft).
- Continual and in-context learning: Kirkpatrick et al. 2017 (PNAS, catastrophic forgetting); Wu et al. 2024 (continual learning survey); Raparthy et al. 2023 (in-context generalization).
- Infrastructure: Harbor and Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al. 2026); Claude Code (Anthropic 2025); Codex CLI (OpenAI 2025).

CODE
Reflection prompt for skill maintenance (Fig 5, App. D, p18): "Based on feedback, update the skill library so the next task benefits: ... 3. Extract Core Skills: Do not memorize this task. Abstract feedback into methods, architectural patterns, or universal domain rules. 4. Maximize Reusability: Keep skills modular and broadly applicable. Avoid task IDs, temporary names, or absolute paths." It also requires each SKILL.md to begin with YAML front matter (name, description), "Otherwise it will not load."

FIGURES
- Fig 3 (p8): skill call frequency and final skill-pool size per domain, GPT-4o vs GPT-5.3-Codex. This is the strongest candidate, because it shows more skills with less reuse for the weaker model in one picture. Caution: the extracted bar values are not clearly mapped to domains, so check the rendered figure before quoting any number from it.
- Fig 1 (p3) is the pipeline overview and is less useful.

NOTE FOR THE TARGET NOTE: the findings bear on "Designing a memory agent" as another instance of the keep-the-raw-trace-versus-distill-a-routine choice. Here keeping the raw context matches distilled skills on average. Distillation only wins on strict-format and procedural tasks, and a weak writer fragments the store. This is close to Agent Workflow Memory and the filesystem-memory comparison already cited in that section, so file it as sharpens.
